# Cyclic support-volume control and a triangular middle-fiber credit

This note proves a planar geometric inequality and a conditional closure of
one actual three-fiber cap configuration. It does not prove the conjecture
for arbitrary three-fiber bodies, and it does not assert that the middle
fiber of a general critical configuration is a triangle.

Write

    v_1=(1,0), v_2=(0,1), v_3=(-1,-1),
    T={x in R^2: v_i.x<=1 for i=1,2,3}.

Then v_1+v_2+v_3=0, T has vertices (1,1),(-2,1),(1,-2), and
|T|=9/2. Here |.| is ordinary planar Lebesgue area, and
h_L(u)=max_{x in L} u.x is the support function of a compact convex set.
All bodies below are full-dimensional planar convex bodies.

## 1. A sharp cyclic support-volume bound

**Lemma 1.** If B is a convex body contained in T, put

    b=|B|, S=sum_i h_B(-v_i), m=S/3.

Then m>0 and

    b/(9/2) <= f(m),                                      (1)

where

    f(m)=m^2                         for 0<m<=1/2,
         1-(2-m)^2/3                for 1/2<=m<=2,
         1                           for m>=2.

Consequently

    6 sqrt(b/(9/2))-S <= 3 sqrt(7)-6 < 3.                 (2)

Both the envelope (1) and the optimized constant in (2) are sharp.

**Proof.** The linear map R(x,y)=(-x-y,x) has determinant 1,
R^3=I, and R^2+R+I=0. It cyclically permutes v_1,v_2,v_3 by
precomposition, and preserves T. Form the Minkowski average

    B_*=(B+RB+R^2B)/3.

Ordinary planar Brunn--Minkowski, applied twice, gives |B_*|>=|B|.
Convexity and R-invariance of T give B_* subset T. Support functions
add under Minkowski addition. Cyclic permutation of the three normals
therefore gives h_{B_*}(-v_i)=S/3=m for every i. In particular

    B_* subset T intersect (-mT).

For an interior point p of B one has h_B(-v_i)>-v_i.p for each i;
summing proves S>0.

The area of T intersect (-mT), divided by |T|, is f(m). To see this
directly, for m<=1/2 the triangle -mT is contained in T. For
1/2<=m<=2, the extra inequalities v_i.x>=-m remove three corner
triangles with disjoint interiors. Each is similar to T with linear
ratio (2-m)/3, so their total relative area is (2-m)^2/3. For
m>=2 the extra inequalities remove nothing. This proves (1).
Choosing B=T intersect (-mT) attains (1), because this set is
R-invariant and has the stated support values in every nontrivial
branch (the branch m>2 is not needed for attainment).

It remains to optimize 6 sqrt(f(m))-3m. On 0<m<=1/2 it equals
3m<=3/2. On m>=2 it is 6-3m<=0. In the middle branch put
x=2-m, so 0<=x<=3/2. The expression is

    6 sqrt(1-x^2/3)+3x-6
      <= sqrt(6^2+(3 sqrt(3))^2)-6
       = 3 sqrt(7)-6,

by Cauchy--Schwarz applied to the unit vector
(sqrt(1-x^2/3),x/sqrt(3)). Equality occurs at
x=3/sqrt(7), hence m=2-3/sqrt(7), which lies in the middle branch.
Since 3 sqrt(7)-6>3/2 and is less than 3, this is the global maximum.
Taking B=T intersect (-(2-3/sqrt(7))T) attains (2). QED.

The map R is an area-preserving continuous-coordinate map. No integer
coordinate is changed, and no Euclidean orthogonality is assumed.

## 2. An aligned triangular middle fiber has strictly larger area

**Theorem 2.** Suppose A,B,K are convex bodies with

    B subset T,    (A+B)/2 subset K,
    K={x: v_i.x>=-t_i for i=1,2,3},

and each cut v_i.x=-1 meets the interior of A. Then

    |K| > (3/2)|B|.                                    (3)

The coefficient 3/2 is sharp as an infimum under these geometric
hypotheses. No assumption on the centroid of K is made.

**Proof.** Write T_K=t_1+t_2+t_3. The displayed description is a
full-dimensional triangle, so T_K>0 and

    k=|K|=T_K^2/2.

For example, setting X=x_1+t_1 and Y=x_2+t_2 changes its inequalities
to X>=0, Y>=0, X+Y<=T_K, which proves the area formula. Each defining
facet is present, and hence h_K(-v_i)=t_i.

Midpoint containment implies

    h_A(-v_i)+h_B(-v_i)<=2t_i.

Properness of the A cut gives h_A(-v_i)>1. Thus, with S and m from
Lemma 1,

    2T_K > 3+S,
    k > (3+S)^2/8.

Combining this with b<= (9/2)f(m) gives

    k/b > (m+1)^2/[4f(m)].                            (4)

For m<=1/2 the last expression is (1+1/m)^2/4>=9/4.
For m>=2 it is (m+1)^2/4>=9/4. In the middle branch,

    (m+1)^2-6f(m)=3(m-1)^2>=0.

Thus (4) is at least 3/2, proving (3).

For sharpness let

    B=T intersect (-T),
    A_e=(1+e)(-T),
    K_e=(1+e/2)(-T),             e>0.

Here |B|=3, all cuts v_i.x=-1 are proper for A_e, and B subset -T
implies (A_e+B)/2 subset K_e. Therefore

    |K_e|/|B|=(3/2)(1+e/2)^2 -> 3/2 as e decreases to 0.

This family establishes sharpness only for the geometric hypotheses
of Theorem 2. It does not assert global criticality of the three caps.
QED.

## 3. The ordinary positive-part cap-cover inequality

For completeness, the precise auxiliary inequality used in the next
section is proved here. The only depth theorem invoked is the ordinary
planar Grünbaum theorem: every closed halfspace containing the centroid
of a planar convex body captures at least 4/9 of its area.

**Lemma 3.** Let L be a planar convex body covered by finitely many
closed halfspaces with nonzero normals and cap areas c_1,...,c_m.
For every alpha>=0,

    |L| <= sum_i(c_i-alpha)_+ +(9/4)alpha.             (5)

**Proof.** Starting with L, visit the halfspaces in order. If its
current captured area exceeds alpha, move its boundary into the
captured side until the deeper cap has area equal to that excess;
retain the opposite closed halfspace. Existence of the threshold
follows from continuity of the cap-area function. Hyperplanes have
zero planar area, so the retained set has exactly alpha area in the
original halfspace. Each removal is at most (c_i-alpha)_+.

The sets retained at all stages are compact and convex. If any stage
has zero area, (5) already follows by the total removal bound. Otherwise
the final retained set L' is again a convex body and has

    |L'|>=|L|-sum_i(c_i-alpha)_+.

Every original halfspace now captures at most alpha of L'. Those
halfspaces cover L', so one contains the centroid of L'. Ordinary
Grünbaum gives (4/9)|L'|<=alpha, proving (5). This argument also
handles alpha=0: a positive-area final body would have a centroid
belonging to a cap of positive area, a contradiction. QED.

This proof is the planar specialization of Section 1 of
`candidate 64b80eee72258d21`.

## 4. Closure for a depth-critical aligned-triangle source

**Theorem 4.** Let C be an actual convex body whose only nonempty
integer fibers are full planar bodies A,K,B at -1,0,1, respectively.
Assume 0 lies in int K, K has the aligned triangular description in
Theorem 2, and all three cuts v_i.x=-1 are proper for A. Suppose
the three ambient closed halfspaces

    H_i={(z,x): v_i.x>=z}

capture zero B-area and attain the same raw mixed halfspace depth Q
at the source (0,0). Then, with M=|A|+|K|+|B|,

    Q > (2/9) M.                                    (6)

No global-maximizer or nonheavy-fiber assumption is necessary. The
comparison Q>=(4/9)|K| follows automatically from the middle cap cover.

**Proof.** Since B has nonempty interior and each B capture has zero
area, B is contained in each opposite closed halfspace v_i.x<=1;
thus B subset T. Actual convexity implies (A+B)/2 subset K. Theorem
2 gives k>3b/2, where a=|A|,k=|K|,b=|B|.

The middle traces cover K, so one contains its ordinary centroid and
captures at least (4/9)k by ordinary Grünbaum. Its middle mass is at
most its total Q. Thus Q>=(4/9)k automatically.

Relabel the A captured areas as u<=v<=w, without changing their
associated normals, and define F=u+v+w/4. All middle captures are
Q-u,Q-v,Q-w because the B captures have zero area. They are positive
since every middle cutting line goes through the interior point 0.
The middle traces cover the entire plane: at every x at least one
v_i.x is nonnegative. Applying (5) to K with alpha=Q-w gives

    k <= (9/4)Q-F.                                  (7)

The A traces v_i.x>=-1 also cover the entire plane. Applying (5) to
A with alpha=u gives

    a <= w+v+u/4,
    delta:=a-u-v <= w-3u/4 <= w.                    (8)

Suppose for contradiction Q<=(2/9)(a+b+k). Substituting (7) and
rearranging yields

    Q <= (4/9)(a+b-F)
       = (4/9)(b+delta-w/4)
       <= 4b/9+w/3.                                (9)

Since w<=Q, (9) gives Q<=2b/3. But the middle comparison and Theorem 2
give Q>=(4/9)k>2b/3, a contradiction. This proves (6). QED.

All mixed measures above are the actual sums of areas on the three
integer fibers. The depth Q refers to every ambient closed halfspace,
including oblique halfspaces. The three displayed halfspaces are assumed
to attain that genuine depth; their equal masses alone are not enough.
The centroid is used only to bound one covering middle cap; no global
maximality premise is needed. Closed-boundary mass causes no issue in
the displayed caps because their continuous normals are nonzero.

## 5. An optional stronger necessary restriction under a bad target

In the configuration of Theorem 4, or with arbitrary full-dimensional K,
genuine depth criticality gives w<=2Q/3. Fix the continuous normal of
the cap whose A area is w. Change only its integer coefficient, keeping
its boundary through the source. In the two opposite large-tilt limits
the captured endpoint pairs tend to (a,0) and (0,b). By continuity,
some tilt equalizes their captured areas to t,t. The source cap q=Q-w
does not change. Global minimality of the original cap, among all
halfspaces through the source, gives w<=2t. The two equal-area endpoint
caps have their actual midpoint contained in the unchanged middle cap;
ordinary Brunn--Minkowski gives q>=t. Thus w<=2q and w<=2Q/3.

Consequently the hypothetical target Q<=2M/9, together with (9),
would force Q<=4b/7. If Q>=(4/9)k, it would also force k<=9b/7.
These are necessary restrictions on a hypothetical bad configuration,
not an assertion that such a configuration exists. This equalization
argument is also recorded in Section 6 of
`candidate fee4b98d94ecbcf2`.

In fact, this proves a stronger quantitative conclusion than (6):

    Q/M > 4/17                                     (10)

under all the hypotheses of Theorem 4. To see this without a
contradiction assumption, equations (7)--(8) give

    M <= b+(9/4)Q+3w/4 <= b+(11/4)Q.

The geometric credit k>3b/2 and Q>=(4/9)k give b<3Q/2, hence
M<(17/4)Q. More generally, for arbitrary K in the same depth-critical
cap configuration one has

    Q/M >= 4k/(11k+9b).                             (11)

Indeed Q/(b+(11/4)Q) is increasing in Q, and Q>=(4/9)k. In
particular k>=9b/7 suffices for the desired weak 2/9 guarantee in
this cap regime. No optimality assertion is made for the bound 4/17.

**Corollary 5 (a quantitative support-triangle deficit).** Retain all
assumptions of Theorem 4 except that K is now an arbitrary planar convex
body. Set

    Kbar={x: v_i.x>=-h_K(-v_i) for i=1,2,3}.

This is the circumscribed triangle with the prescribed three outer
normals. If Q<=2M/9, then

    |K|/|Kbar| < 6/7.                               (12)

In particular more than one seventh of the area of this actual support
triangle is missing from K. With m from Lemma 1, the sharper bound is

    |K|/|Kbar| < 36 f(m)/[7(m+1)^2].                (13)

Indeed Kbar contains K and satisfies all geometric hypotheses of
Theorem 2, so |Kbar|>3b/2. The bad target, the unchanged cap profiles,
equalization, and automatic middle comparison imply k<=9b/7, as just
proved. Division gives (12). Using the stronger intermediate inequality
|Kbar|/b>(m+1)^2/[4f(m)] gives (13). The triangle Kbar is compact and
full-dimensional because the three outer normals form a positive
circuit and Kbar contains the convex body K. No assertion about a
triangle approximation or a limiting sequence is involved.

## Scope

The geometric inequalities use arbitrary convex planar bodies B, with no
rationality, facet-complexity, or symmetry assumption. The middle-fiber
triangle assumption in Theorems 2 and 4 is explicit and indispensable to
the present proof. Nothing here proves that an arbitrary OC-critical
middle fiber has that shape, or converts the support-triangle area
deficit in Corollary 5 into a contradiction for arbitrary K.
